verses.zh: 有一个人，名叫亚拿尼亚，同他的妻子撒非喇卖了田产，
verses.en: Now a man named Ananias, together with Sapphira his wife, sold a piece of property.
verses.commentary:
5:1 "Ananias" The full Hebrew name would have been Hananiah, which means "YHWH has graciously
given" or "YHWH is gracious" (BDB 337).

▣ Sapphira" This was Ananias' wife. The name in Aramaic means "beautiful." They were
both believers.

verses.zh: 把价银私自留下几分，他的妻子也知道，其余的几分拿来放在使徒脚前。
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] kept back for himself part of the proceeds with his wife’s knowledge; he brought[NOTE:2] only part of it and placed it at the apostles’ feet.
notes: Grk “And he.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English style to use shorter sentences, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
The participle ἐνέγκας (enenkas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
verses.commentary:
5:2 kept back" This same rare VERB (nosphizomai; to set apart for one's own use) is
used in the Septuagint (LXX) of Joshua 7:1 to describe the sin of Achan. F. F. Bruce, in his commentary on Acts (NIC)
has made the comment that Ananias was to the early church what Achan was to the Conquest. This sin had the potential
of hurting the entire church. This term is also used in Titus 2:10 of slaves stealing from their masters.

▣ "bringing a portion of it, he laid it at the apostles' feet" This mimics what Barnabas did in
Acts 4:37. This couple had the freedom to sell or not to sell their personal property (cf. Acts 5:4). They
had the freedom to give some or all of it to the Lord's work. They did not have the right to give part,
but claim they gave all. Their motives and duplicitous actions revealed their heart (cf. Acts 5:4c;
Luke 21:14). God looks at the heart (cf. 1 Sam. 16:7; 1 Kgs. 8:39; 1 Chr. 28:9; Prov. 21:2; Jer. 17:10;
Luke 16:15; Acts 1:24; Rom. 8:27).

verses.zh: 彼得说：「亚拿尼亚！为甚么撒但充满了你的心，叫你欺哄圣灵，把田地的价银私自留下几分呢？
verses.en: But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled[NOTE:1] your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and keep back for yourself part of the proceeds from the sale of[NOTE:2] the land?
notes: This is a good example of the Greek verb fill (πληρόω, plēroō) meaning “to exercise control over someone’s thought and action” (cf. Eph 5:18).

The words “from the sale of” are not in the Greek text, but are supplied to clarify the meaning, since the phrase “proceeds from the land” could possibly be understood as crops rather than money from the sale.
verses.commentary:
5:3 "Satan. . .Holy Spirit" This shows the presence of the two spiritual forces which are active
in our world and in our lives. In Eph. 2:2-3 (cf. James. 4) are listed the three enemies of post-Genesis 3
humanity:

- the fallen world system

- a personal tempter

- our fallen human nature

SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "filled" This is the same word used of the Spirit (cf. Eph. 5:18). Filling requires
cooperation! We are filled with something (see full note at Acts 5:17)! Satan tempts, but we are still
responsible (cf. Luke 22:3-6). I recommend the book Three Crucial Questions About Spiritual Warfare,
by Clinton E. Arnold. Surprisingly there is continuing satanic influence in the lives of believers
(cf. Romans 7; Eph. 6:10-19; 1 John 5:18-19). See fuller notes at Acts 2:4 and 3:10.

This phrase (i.e., filled your heart") may be a Hebrew idiom (cf. Esther 7:5; Eccl. 8:11; 9:3).
Many scholars assume an Aramaic original to the early chapters of Acts.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FILLED WITH THE SPIRIT

▣ "to lie to the Holy Spirit" They lied to Peter and the church, but in reality they lied
to the Spirit. Theologically this is very similar to Jesus asking Paul on the road to Damascus, "Why are
you persecuting Me?" (cf. Acts 9:4). Paul was persecuting individual believers, but Jesus took it personally,
as does the Spirit here. This should be a word of warning to modern believers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE NT

verses.zh: 田地还没有卖，不是你自己的吗？既卖了，价银不是你作主吗？你怎么心里起这意念呢？你不是欺哄人，是欺哄　神了。」
verses.en: Before it was sold,[NOTE:1] did it not[NOTE:2] belong to you? And when it was sold, was the money[NOTE:3] not at your disposal? How have you thought up this deed in your heart?[NOTE:4] You have not lied to people[NOTE:5] but to God!”
notes: Grk “Remaining to you.”
The negative interrogative particle οὐχί (ouchi) expects a positive reply to this question and the following one (“And when it was sold, was it not at your disposal?”).
Grk “it”; the referent of the pronoun (the money generated from the sale of the land) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “How is it that you have [or Why have you] placed this deed in your heart?” Both of these literal translations differ from the normal way of expressing the thought in English.

Grk “to men.” If Peter’s remark refers only to the apostles, the translation “to men” would be appropriate. But if (as is likely) the action was taken to impress the entire congregation (who would presumably have witnessed the donation or been aware of it) then the more general “to people” is more appropriate, since the audience would have included both men and women.
verses.commentary:
5:4 This verse has two questions that expect "yes" answers. This is a grammatical feature, not
an interpretive issue.

▣ "You have not lied to men but to God" It was not that they kept part of the money, but that
they lied to make themselves look spiritual (lit, "to men," to the Apostles or to the church) . Notice that even a kind,
generous act, which is done with a bad motive, is a sin (cf. Rom. 14:23c).

Notice that the Holy Spirit mentioned in Acts 5:3 here is called God. See Millard Erickson, Christian
Theology, 2nd ed., pp. 873-875.

verses.zh: 亚拿尼亚听见这话，就仆倒，断了气；听见的人都甚惧怕。
verses.en: When Ananias heard these words he collapsed and died, and great fear gripped[NOTE:1] all who heard about it.
notes: Or “fear came on,” “fear seized”; Grk “fear happened to.”
verses.commentary:
5:5 "fell down and breathed his last" In the ancient world one's last breath was evidence that the
spirit of the person had left (cf. Jgds. 4:2; Ezek. 21:7 in the LXX). This rare term is found in the NT
only in Acts (cf. Acts 5:4,10; 12:23). This is an example of temporal judgment. This is similar to God's
judgment on Aaron's sons in Leviticus 10. Sin is serious to God. It cost a life (cf. 2 Kgs. 14:6;
Ezek. 18:4,20).

▣ "a great fear came over all" This possibly was the purpose of this temporal judgment. This
would be analogous to the OT deaths of Nadab and Abihu of Leviticus 10 and Uzzah of 2 Samuel 6. Based
on 1 Cor. 11:30; James 5:20; and 1 John 5:16-17, it is possible to assume that some sins by believers
result in an early death. It is hard to keep the balance between the holiness of God (transcendence)
and Fatherhood of God (immanence); justice and grace.

verses.zh: 有些少年人起来，把他包裹，抬出去埋葬了。
verses.en: So the young men came,[NOTE:1] wrapped him up,[NOTE:2] carried him out, and buried[NOTE:3] him.
notes: Or “arose.”

The translation “wrapped up” for συνέστειλαν (sunesteilan) is suggested by L&N 79.119, but another interpretation is possible. The same verb could also be translated “removed” (see L&N 15.200), although that sense appears somewhat redundant and out of sequence with the following verb and participle (“carried him out and buried him”).
Buried. Same day burial was a custom in the Jewish world of the first century (cf. also Deut 21:23).
verses.commentary:
5:6 "they buried him" Jews of the first century did not practice embalming (they still do not),
probably because of Gen. 3:19 (cf. Ps. 103:14; 104:29). A person had to be buried quickly, usually
within one day.

Because of the offense there was no memorial service or other Christian burial rites.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

verses.zh: 约过了三小时，他的妻子进来，还不知道这事。
verses.en: After an interval of about three hours,[NOTE:1] his wife came in, but she did not know[NOTE:2] what had happened.
notes: Grk “It happened that after an interval of about three hours.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

Grk “came in, not knowing.” The participle has been translated with concessive or adversative force: “although she did not know.” In English, the adversative conjunction (“but”) conveys this nuance more smoothly.
verses.commentary:
5:7 "about three hours" This shows the vividness of the account by an eyewitness. Luke's writing
is characterized by this attention to details. It reflects both his writing style and research methods
(i.e., interviews with eyewitnesses).

verses.zh: 彼得对她说：「你告诉我，你们卖田地的价银就是这些吗？」她说：「就是这些。」
verses.en: Peter said to her, “Tell me, were the two of you[NOTE:1] paid this amount[NOTE:2] for the land?” Sapphira[NOTE:3] said, “Yes, that much.”
notes: The words “the two of” are not in the Greek text, but have been supplied to indicate that the verb (ἀπέδοσθε, apedosthe) is plural and thus refers to both Ananias and Sapphira.
Grk “so much,” “as much as this.”
Grk “She”; the referent (Sapphira) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
verses.commentary: 5:8 The lie, the pretense continues! See Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 519-521.

verses.zh: 彼得说：「你们为甚么同心试探主的灵呢？埋葬你丈夫之人的脚已到门口，他们也要把你抬出去。」
verses.en: Peter then told her, “Why have you agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Look! The feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out!”
verses.commentary:
5:9 "test" In a round about sense, this was a test of the presence and power of the Holy Spirit,
God the Father's personal presence on earth. There are temporal consequences, as well as eternal
consequences for challenging the Spirit! These two did not realize that it was the Spirit they were
lying to, but Peter did.

There are two Greek terms used to denote a test. This one connotes "to test with a view
toward destruction." This possibly reflects Exod. 17:2 and Deut. 6:16, where these texts warn against
tempting/testing YHWH (cf. Ps. 78:18,41,56).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK TERMS FOR TESTING AND THEIR CONNOTATIONS

▣ "door" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: "DOOR" IN THE NT

verses.zh: 妇人立刻仆倒在彼得脚前，断了气。那些少年人进来，见她已经死了，就抬出去，埋在她丈夫旁边。
verses.en: At once[NOTE:1] she collapsed at his feet and died. So when the young men came in, they found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her beside her husband.
notes: Grk “And at once.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
verses.commentary:
5:10 The term used to describe "the young men" (neōteroi) in Acts 5:6 is different
from the term neanikoi in Acts 5:10. It is uncertain whether this is just authorial variety or
a different group of young men in the church. Both Greek words come from the same root word (neos).

verses.zh: 全教会和听见这事的人都甚惧怕。
verses.en: Great[NOTE:1] fear gripped[NOTE:2] the whole church[NOTE:3] and all who heard about these things.
notes: Grk “And great.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Or “fear came on,” “fear seized”; Grk “fear happened to.”
This is the first occurrence of the term church (ἐκκλησία, ekklēsia) in Acts. It refers to an assembly of people.
verses.commentary:
5:11 "great fear. . .over all who heard of these things" Luke uses the common word phobos
several times in this same general sense (cf. Luke 1:69; 3:37; Acts 19:17).

- For believers it is a sense of reverence, respect, and awe.

- But for unbelievers it is a sense of foreboding, fear, and terror (cf. Luke 12:4-5; Heb. 10:31).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR

▣ "church" This is the first time this term is used in Acts, although it is in the Textus
Receptus at Acts 2:47.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH (ekklēsia)

verses.zh: 主藉使徒的手在民间行了许多神迹奇事；他们（或译：信的人）都同心合意地在所罗门的廊下。
verses.en: Now many miraculous signs[NOTE:1] and wonders came about among the people through the hands of the apostles. By[NOTE:2] common consent[NOTE:3] they were all meeting together in Solomon’s Portico.[NOTE:4]
notes: The miraculous nature of these signs is implied in the context.
Grk “And by.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
Or “With one mind.”

Or “colonnade”; Grk “stoa.”sn Solomon’s Portico was a covered walkway formed by rows of columns supporting a roof and open on the inner side facing the center of the temple complex. Located beside the Court of the Gentiles, it was a very public area.
verses.commentary:
5:12-16 This is a brief summary, which is so characteristic of the book of Acts (cf. Acts 2:43-47
and 4:32-35). See Introduction, "Purpose and Structure," B.

5:12 "many signs and wonders" This is an IMPERFECT PASSIVE
(deponent) INDICATIVE. These two terms appear in Peter's quote from Joel 2 in Acts 2:19.
Miracles were repeatedly performed (cf. Acts 2:43; 4:30; 5:12; 6:8; 7:36; 8:13; 14:3; 15:12). Remember that
the miraculous is not automatically a sign of deity (cf. Matt. 24:24; and 2 Thess. 2:9), but it was and
is a way to confirm the new Christian message, which was so radically different from the focus and
emphasis of Judaism.

▣ "they were all in one accord" See note at Acts 1:14. It is important to Luke to emphasize
this again and again. It was an ideal that did not last long!

▣ "in Solomon's portico" This was an open colonnade within the temple area along the eastern
wall of the Court of the Gentiles. Jesus often taught there also (cf. John 10:23). This was the site of
Peter and John's first arrest.

verses.zh: 其余的人没有一个敢贴近他们，百姓却尊重他们。
verses.en: None of the rest dared to join them,[NOTE:1] but the people held them in high honor.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “to associate with them.” The group was beginning to have a controversial separate identity. People were cautious about joining them. The next verse suggests that the phrase “none of the rest” in this verse is rhetorical hyperbole.
Or “the people thought very highly of them.”
verses.commentary:
5:13

NASB
"none of the rest dared to associate with them"

NKJV, NRSV
"none of the rest dared join them"

TEV, REB
"Nobody outside the group dared join them"

NJB
"No one else dared to join them"

Peshitta
"None of the unbelievers dared to interfere with them"

This is an unusual phrase. It seems to describe the negative side of "fear." There
are several groups designated in this context (cf. Acts 5:12-16). For most, the events were a draw to
faith in Christ (cf. #5 and possibly #6 and #7) or a confirmation of faith in Christ (i.e., #3).

- the Apostles, Acts 5:12

- the people, Acts 5:12,13

- the believers (i.e., in one accord in Solomon's portico), Acts 5:12

- the rest (i.e., the Jewish leadership), Acts 5:13

- new believers, Acts 5:14

- the sick of Jerusalem, Acts 5:15

- the sick and possessed from the surrounding villages, Acts 5:16

The PRESENT MIDDLE INFINITIVE "to associate" is literally "to glue." Luke
uses this term often, but in a wide variety of senses. Here it refers to their not becoming part of the
new group (i.e., believers in Jesus as the promised Messiah).

verses.zh: 信而归主的人越发增添，连男带女很多。
verses.en: More and more believers in the Lord were added to their number,[NOTE:1] crowds of both men and women.
notes: Or “More and more believers were added to the Lord.”
verses.commentary:
5:14 "believers" This is a PRESENT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, which implies an ongoing
action.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FAITH, BELIEVE, OR TRUST

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK VERB TENSES USED FOR SALVATION

NASB, TEV, NJB, NIV, Peshitta, REB
"in the Lord"

NKJV, NRSV
"to the Lord"

This grammatical form (i.e., eight case system) can be understood as DATIVE
("to") or LOCATIVE ("in"). I think it is a way to show that believers belong to the Lord.
We are His possession, and He is ours! The Special Topic below denotes the different PREPOSITIONS
related to "bellieve," found in John's writings.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JOHN'S USE OF THE VERB "BELIEVE"

▣ "women" Luke especially highlights "women," both in the Gospel and Acts (i.e., Acts 1:14; 8:12;
16:1,13; 17:4,12,34; 18:2; 21:5). Jesus brings a new sense of dignity and worth to women and children.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

▣ "were constantly added to their number" Luke often used summary statements of the
growth of the church (cf. Acts 2:47; 5:14; 6:7; 9:31; 12:24; 16:5; 19:20). See Introduction, "Purpose and Structure," B.

verses.zh: 甚至有人将病人抬到街上，放在床上或褥子上，指望彼得过来的时候，或者得他的影儿照在甚么人身上。
verses.en: Thus[NOTE:1] they even carried the sick out into the streets and put them on cots and pallets, so that when Peter came by at least his shadow would fall on some of them.
notes: This is a continuation of the preceding sentence in Greek, but because this would produce an awkward sentence in English, a new sentence was begun here in the translation.
verses.commentary:
5:15 "when Peter came by at least his shadow" Miracles at this stage were common as a way of
confirming the gospel. Peter was the obvious spokesman for the Apostles. This same type of confirming,
healing also occurred through Paul (cf. Acts 19:12).

As interpreters we must remember that these miracle signs were given to

- show the compassion of God

- show the truth of the gospel

- show who were the God-called leaders

These signs were given in a particular culture, for a specific purpose. Because God did it
there, it does not automatically mean that He will do the same in every period of history in every culture.
Not that God is not active in every age nor less compassionate, but that the people of God must walk by
faith and not by sight! Miracles continue, but salvation of sinners must be the greatest goal, not physical
healing for those who will still die!

It seems to me that God has not changed. His character, power, compassion, and desire for
all to be saved remains the same, but looking at history theologically, there are two major periods of
intense, supernatural signs, both from God and from Satan.

- surrounding the time of the incarnation and development of the early church

- preceding the end-time events when believers will be under terrible persecution

I would like to quote A. T. Robertson, Word Pictures in the New Testament,
vol. III, p. 62

"There was, of course, no virtue or power in Peter's shadow. That
was faith with superstition, of course, just as similar cases in the Gospels occur
(Matt. 9:20; Mark 6:56; John 9:5) and the use of Paul's handkerchief (Acts 19:12).
God honours even superstitious faith if it is real faith in him. Few people are
wholly devoid of superstition."

verses.zh: 还有许多人带着病人和被污鬼缠磨的，从耶路撒冷四围的城邑来，全都得了医治。
verses.en: A crowd of people from the towns around Jerusalem[NOTE:1] also came together, bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits.[NOTE:2] They[NOTE:3] were all[NOTE:4] being healed.
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Unclean spirits refers to evil spirits.

Literally a relative pronoun, “who.” In English, however, a relative clause (“bringing the sick and those troubled by unclean spirits, who were all being healed”) could be understood to refer only to the second group (meaning only those troubled by unclean spirits were being healed) or even that the unclean spirits were being healed. To avoid this ambiguity the pronoun “they” was used to begin a new English sentence.
They were all being healed. Note how the healings that the apostles provided were comprehensive in their consistency.
verses.commentary:
5:16 "they were all being healed" This is an IMPERFECT PASSIVE INDICATIVE, which
asserts each one was healed (the agent is unexpressed, but probably by Jesus or the Spirit) one at a time, over
and over and over, until none were left!

This is a summary type statement. Are we to take it literally (i.e., every single one)?
Jesus required faith or used the healing to

- train the disciples

- cause the crowds to listen

It is shocking to me that not all those healed in the NT were simultaneously "saved"
(i.e., trust Christ and have eternal life). Physical healing is a poor substitute for spiritual
salvation. Miracles are only truly helpful if they bring us to God. All humans live in a fallen world.
Bad things happen. God often chooses not to intervene, but this says nothing about His love and concern.
Be careful of demanding that God act miraculously every time in this current evil age. He is sovereign
and we do not know the full implications of any given situation. A booklet by a charismatic author, Gordon Fee,
that has really helped me think through the issue biblically, is "The Disease of the Health, Wealth Gospels,"

At this point I would like to add my commentary notes from 2 Tim. 4:20 about Paul
and physical healing (see www.freebiblecommentary.org ):

"There are so many questions we would like to ask the NT writers. One
subject all believers think about is physical healing. In Acts (cf. Acts 19:12;
28:7-9) Paul is able to heal, but here and in 2 Cor. 12:7-10 and Phil. 2:25-30,
he seems unable. Why are some healed and not all, and is there a time window connected
to healing which has closed?

I surely believe in a supernatural, compassionate Father who has
and does heal physically as well as spiritually, but why is this healing aspect
seemingly present and then noticeably absent? I do not think that it is connected
to human faith, for surely Paul had faith (cf. 2 Corinthians 12). I feel that
healing and believing miracles affirmed the truthfulness and validity of the gospel,
which it still does in areas of the world where it is first proclaimed. However, I feel
that God wants us to walk by faith and not by sight. Also, physical illness is often
allowed in believer's lives (1) as temporal punishment for sin; (2) as consequences
of life in a fallen world; and (3) to help believers mature spiritually. My problem
is that I never know which one is involved! My prayer for God's will to be done in
each case is not a lack of faith but a sincere attempt to allow the gracious,
compassionate God to work His will in each life."

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEALING

▣ "unclean spirits" The NT always makes a distinction between mental and physical illness vs. demon
possession.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEMONIC
(unclean spirits)

SPECIAL TOPIC: EXORCISM

verses.zh: 大祭司和他的一切同人，就是撒都该教门的人，都起来，满心忌恨，
verses.en: Now the high priest rose up, and all those with him (that is, the religious party of the Sadducees[NOTE:1]),[NOTE:2] and they were filled with jealousy.[NOTE:3]
notes: See the note on Sadducees in 4:1.
This is a parenthetical note by the author.

Filled with jealousy. In Acts, the term “jealousy” (ζήλος, zēlos) occurs only here and in Acts 13:45. It is a key term in Judaism for religiously motivated rage (1 Macc 2:24; 1QH 14:13-15; m. Sanhedrin 9:5). It was a zeal motivated by a desire to maintain the purity of the faith.
verses.commentary:
5:17 "the high priest. . .his associates (that is the sect of the Sadducees)" Luke is adding an editorial comment to explain
to Gentile readers that the Sanhedrin was dominated by the high priest and Sadducean sect of Judaism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SANHEDRIN

SPECIAL TOPIC: SADDUCEES

▣ "they were filled with jealousy" The Greek word "jealous" simply means "to boil." Therefore, context
must tell us it is zealousness or jealousy. This shows the true motivation of the religious leaders, jealousy! This term is
in Acts only here and Acts 13:45. The NET Bible, p. 1983, asserts that it denotes "religiously motivated rage" (i.e., Macc. 2:24;
IQH 14:13-15). So it could deonte

- jealousy of Jesus' Apostles' popularity with the people (v. 26)

- theological anger over the Apostles' actions in Jesus' name (i.e., a theological issue, cf. Matt. 26:65)

In Luke's Gospel Jesus' main enemies were the Pharisees, but in Acts His followers' main
enemies were the Sadducees.

The VERB "filled" is used in a variety of ways by Luke to show what
characterizes or describes a person or personified entity.

- John the Baptist, even before his birth, was filled with the Holy Spirit - Luke 1:15

- Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit - Luke 1:41

- Zacharias was filled with the Holy Spirit -Luke 1:67

- all in the Synagogue who heard Jesus speak were filled with rage - Luke 4:28

- those in the house where the paralytic was lowered through the roof were filled with
fear - Luke 5:26

- Pharisees and Scribes traveling with Jesus on a Sabbath were filled with rage - Luke 6:11

- those in the upper room on Pentecost were filled with the Holy Spirit - Acts 2:4

- those who heard Peter speak in the temple were filled with amazement - Acts 3:10

- Peter speaking before the Sanhedrin was filled with the Holy Spirit - Acts 4:8

- all in the upper room were filled with the Holy Spirit - Acts 4:31

- Satan filled Ananias' and Sapphira's hearts - Acts 5:3

- Peter and John spoke to the Sanhedrin again and they were filled with jealousy - Acts 5:17

- Jerusalem filled with the gospel - Acts 5:28

- the seven full of the Spirit and wisdom - Acts 6:3

- Stephen full of faith and the Holy Spirit - Acts 6:5,8; 7:55

- Ananias lays hands on Saul/Paul and he is filled with the Holy Spirit - Acts 9:17

- Paul preaches filled with the Spirit - Acts 13:9

- Jews in the crowd who Paul preached to were filled with jealousy - Acts 13:45

- the disciples were continually filled with joy and the Holy Spirit - Acts 13:52

- Ephesus was filled with confusion - Acts 19:29

In the presence of the gospel what are you "filled" with?

verses.zh: 就下手拿住使徒，收在外监。
verses.en: They[NOTE:1] laid hands on[NOTE:2] the apostles and put them in a public jail.
notes: Grk “jealousy, and they.” In the Greek text this is a continuation of the previous sentence, but a new sentence has been started here in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Or “they arrested.”
verses.commentary:
5:18 These first chapters in Acts show the problems faced by the early church. The problems differ
from age to age, culture to culture, but God is for us, with us, and empowers us to overcome (cf. John 16:33;
Rom. 8:37; 1 Cor. 15:57; 1 John 5:4,5). Nothing-prison, attempted humiliation, threats, etc.-can
rob believers of the presence and peace of Christ (cf. Rom. 8:31-39).

verses.zh: 但主的使者夜间开了监门，领他们出来，
verses.en: But during the night an angel of the Lord[NOTE:1] opened[NOTE:2] the doors of the prison,[NOTE:3] led them out,[NOTE:4] and said,
notes: Or “the angel of the Lord.” Linguistically, “angel of the Lord” is the same in both testaments (and thus, he is either “an angel of the Lord” or “the angel of the Lord” in both testaments). For arguments and implications, see ExSyn 252; M. J. Davidson, “Angels,” DJG, 9; W. G. MacDonald argues for “an angel” in both testaments: “Christology and ‘The Angel of the Lord’,” Current Issues in Biblical and Patristic Interpretation, 324-35.
Grk “opening the doors of the prison.” The participle ἀνοίξας (anoixas) has been translated as a finite verb due to the requirements of contemporary English style.
Greek φυλακῆς (phulakēs), a different word from the one in v. 18 (τήρησις, tērēsis, “jail”).

Led them out. The action by God served to vindicate the apostles. It showed that whatever court the Jewish leaders represented, they did not represent God.tn Or “brought them out.” Grk “and leading them out, said.” The participle ἐξαγαγών (exagagōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
verses.commentary:
5:19 "an angel of the Lord" This phrase is used two ways in the OT.

- an angel (cf. Gen. 24:7,40; Exod. 23:20-23; 32:34; Num. 22:22; Jdgs. 5:23; 1 Sam. 24:16;
1 Chr. 21:15ff; Zech. 1:28)

- as a way of referring to a physical manifestation of YHWH (cf. Gen. 16:7-13; 22:11-15; 31:11,13; 48:15-16; Exod. 3:2,4;
13:21; 14:19; Jdgs. 2:1; 6:22-24; 13:3-23; Zech. 3:1-2)

Luke uses the phrase often (cf. Luke 1:11,13; 2:9; Acts 5:19; 7:30; 8:26; 12:7,11,23;
10:3; 27:23), but in the sense of #1 above. The NT does not use sense #2, except in Acts 8:26 and 29,
where, "an angel of the Lord" is paralleled to the Holy Spirit.

SPECIAL TOPIC: The Angel of the Lord

▣ "opened the gates of the prison" This is similar to Paul and Silas' experience at Philippi
(cf. Acts 16:26). In many ways the life of Peter is paralleled in Paul. This may have been Luke's
literary intentionality. This would clearly demonstrate Paul's Apostleship.

verses.zh: 说：「你们去站在殿里，把这生命的道都讲给百姓听。」
verses.en: “Go and stand in the temple courts[NOTE:1] and proclaim[NOTE:2] to the people all the words of this life.”
notes: Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.
Or “speak.”
verses.commentary:
5:20 "Go, stand and speak" These function as three IMPERATIVES.

- Go, PRESENT MIDDLE (deponent) IMPERATIVE

- Stand, AORIST PASSIVE PARTICIPLE used as an IMPERATIVE
(Friberg's, Analytical Greek New Testament, p. 379)

- Speak, PRESENT ACTIVE IMPERATIVE

The angel had an evangelistic mission for the early church (and for today's church).

▣ "speak to the people" This was the major thrust of the Apostles' ministry (i.e., Acts 1:8, "My witnesses").
Boldness, not fear, characterizes their new Spirit-filled lives.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOLDNESS

NASB
"the whole message of the Life"

NKJV, Peshitta
"all the words of this life"

NRSV
"the whole message about this life"

TEV, REB
"all about this new life"

REB
"all about this new Life"

This phrase is speaking about the new life (zōe, eternal life) found only
in the gospel of Jesus Christ. They had been freed both spiritually (salvation) and physically (out of prison).
Now they were to witness the gospel to all (cf. Matt. 28:18-20; Luke 24:47; Acts 1:8)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

verses.zh: 使徒听了这话，天将亮的时候就进殿里去教训人。大祭司和他的同人来了，叫齐公会的人和以色列族的众长老，就差人到监里去，要把使徒提出来。
verses.en: When they heard this, they entered the temple courts[NOTE:1] at daybreak and began teaching.[NOTE:2] Now when the high priest and those who were with him arrived, they summoned the Sanhedrin[NOTE:3]—that is, the whole high council[NOTE:4] of the Israelites[NOTE:5]—and sent to the jail to have the apostles[NOTE:6] brought before them.[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “the temple.” See the note on the same phrase in the preceding verse.
The imperfect verb ἐδίδασκον (edidaskon) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.
Or “the council” (the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews).

A hendiadys (two different terms referring to a single thing) is likely here (a reference to a single legislative body rather than two separate ones) because the term γερουσίαν (gerousian) is used in both 1 Macc 12:6 and Josephus, Ant. 13.5.8 (13.166) to refer to the Sanhedrin.
Grk “sons of Israel.”
Grk “have them”; the referent (the apostles) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The words “before them” are not in the Greek text but are implied.
verses.commentary:
5:21 Notice that being supernaturally freed did not imply that they would not be imprisoned
again. Even God's provision does not mean that all difficulties will be solved or removed in
ministry (cf. Matt. 5:10-12; Rom. 8:17; 1 Pet. 4:12-16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHY DO CHRISTIANS SUFFER?

▣ "the Council. . .the Senate of the sons of Israel" To whom does "the Senate" refer?

- Curtis Vaughan, in Acts, pp. 39-40, says it was the elders of Jerusalem who were not members of
the Sanhedrin at that present time (cf. M. R. Vincent, Word Studies, Vol. 1, p. 234).

- The NASB and NIV translations assume that "Council" and "Senate" are synonymous (i.e., hendiadys).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SANHEDRIN

verses.zh: 但差役到了，不见他们在监里，就回来禀报说：
verses.en: But the officers[NOTE:1] who came for them[NOTE:2] did not find them in the prison, so they returned and reported,[NOTE:3]
notes: The Greek term ὑπηρέτης (hupēretēs) generally means “servant,” but in the NT is used for many different types of servants, like attendants to a king, the officers of the Sanhedrin (as here), assistants to magistrates, and (especially in the Gospel of John) Jewish guards in the Jerusalem temple (see L&N 35.20).
The words “for them” are not in the Greek text but are implied.
Grk “reported, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in English and has not been translated.

verses.zh: 「我们看见监牢关得极妥当，看守的人也站在门外；及至开了门，里面一个人都不见。」
verses.en: “We found the jail locked securely and the guards standing at the doors, but when we opened them,[NOTE:1] we found no one inside.”
notes: The word “them” is not in the Greek text, but is implied. Direct objects in Greek were often omitted when clear from the context, but must be supplied for the modern English reader.
verses.commentary:
5:23 "locked" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE. The idea was that the prison
doors were secure and the guards set (PERFECT ACTIVE PARTICIPLE), but the prisoners were gone.

verses.zh: 守殿官和祭司长听见这话，心里犯难，不知这事将来如何。
verses.en: Now when the commander[NOTE:1] of the temple guard[NOTE:2] and the chief priests heard this report,[NOTE:3] they were greatly puzzled concerning it,[NOTE:4] wondering what this could[NOTE:5] be.
notes: Or “captain.”
Grk “the official of the temple,” a title for the commander of the Jewish soldiers guarding the temple (thus the translation, “the commander of the temple guard”). See L&N 37.91.
Grk “heard these words.”
Grk “concerning them,” agreeing with the plural antecedent “these words.” Since the phrase “these words” was translated as the singular “this report,” the singular “concerning it” is used here.
The optative verb here expresses confused uncertainty.
verses.commentary:
5:24 "the captain of the temple guard and the chief priests" The first person spoken of was the Levitical leader of the
temple guard. It was a very high and respected position.

It is susrprising that "high priests" is PLURAL here but SINGULAR in
v. 17. In reality, the position of "high priest" was purchased from the Roman authorities. In Jesus' day several from the
same family (i.e., Annas) served in succession (i.e., Luke 3:2; John 18:13-14; Acts 4:6).

▣ "they were greatly perplexed" Luke uses this term several times. It is an intensified form
of aporeō (cf. Luke 24:4; Acts 25:20) with dia (cf. Luke 9:7; Acts 2:12; 5:24; 10:17).
Its basic meaning is doubt, uncertainty, or perplexity.

▣ "as to what would come of this" The grammatical form of the phrase is an incomplete
FOURTH CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE (an plus AORIST MIDDLE [deponent]
OPTATIVE). The OPTATIVE MOOD expresses perplexity (cf. Luke 1:61-62; 3:15;
8:9; 15:26; 22:23; Acts 5:24; 8:31; 10:17; 21:33, see James Allen Hewett, New Testament Greek, p. 195).

verses.zh: 有一个人来禀报说：「你们收在监里的人，现在站在殿里教训百姓。」
verses.en: But someone came and reported to them, “Look! The men you put in prison are standing in the temple courts[NOTE:1] and teaching[NOTE:2] the people!”
notes: Grk “the temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper, and has been translated accordingly.
Obeying God (see v. 29), the apostles were teaching again (4:18-20; 5:20). They did so despite the risk.

verses.zh: 于是守殿官和差役去带使徒来，并没有用强暴，因为怕百姓用石头打他们。
verses.en: Then the commander[NOTE:1] of the temple guard[NOTE:2] went with the officers[NOTE:3] and brought the apostles[NOTE:4] without the use of force[NOTE:5] (for they were afraid of being stoned by the people).[NOTE:6]
notes: Or “captain.”
Grk “the official [of the temple],” a title for the commander of the Jewish soldiers guarding the temple (thus the translation, “the commander of the temple guard”). See L&N 37.91.
The Greek term ὑπηρέτης (hupēretēs) generally means “servant,” but in the NT is used for many different types of servants. See the note on the word “officers” in v. 22.
Grk “brought them”; the referent (the apostles) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “without violence.” It is clear, as well, that the apostles did not resist arrest.
Grk “for they feared lest they be stoned by the people.” The translation uses a less awkward English equivalent. This is an explanatory note by the author.
verses.commentary:
5:26 "they were afraid of the people, that they might be stoned" This showed the popularity of the
early church (cf. Acts 5:13; 2:47; 4:21) and the source of the continuing jealousy of the Jewish leaders.

SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH

verses.zh: 带到了，便叫使徒站在公会前；大祭司问他们说：
verses.en: When they had brought them, they stood them before the council,[NOTE:1] and the high priest questioned[NOTE:2] them,
notes: Or “the Sanhedrin” (the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews).
Or “interrogated,” “asked.”

verses.zh: 「我们不是严严地禁止你们，不可奉这名教训人吗？你们倒把你们的道理充满了耶路撒冷，想要叫这人的血归到我们身上！」
verses.en: saying, “We gave[NOTE:1] you strict orders[NOTE:2] not to teach in this name.[NOTE:3] Look,[NOTE:4] you have filled Jerusalem[NOTE:5] with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man’s blood[NOTE:6] on us!”
notes: ‡ The majority of mss, including a few significant witnesses (א2 D E [Ψ] 1739 M sy sa), have the negative particle οὐ (ou) here, effectively turning the high priest’s words into a question: “Did we not give you strict orders not to teach in this name?” But the earliest and most significant mss, along with some others (P74 א* A B 1175 lat bo), lack the particle, making this a strong statement rather than a question. Scribes may have been tempted to omit the particle to strengthen the contrast between official Judaism and the new faith, but the fact that v. 27 introduces the quotation with ἐπηρώτησεν (epērōtēsen, “he questioned”) may well have prompted scribes to add οὐ to convert the rebuke into a question. Further, that excellent witnesses affirm the shorter reading is sufficient ground for accepting it as most probably authentic. NA28 includes the particle in brackets, indicating some doubt as to its authenticity.
Grk “We commanded you with a commandment” (a Semitic idiom that is emphatic).
The name (i.e., person) of Jesus is the constant issue of debate.
Grk “And behold.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English style to use shorter sentences, καί (kai) has not been translated here.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
To bring this man’s blood on us is an idiom meaning “you intend to make us guilty of this man’s death.”
verses.commentary:
5:28

NASB, NRSV, TEV
"strict orders"

NKJV, Peshitta
"strictly command"

NJB
"strong warning"

REB
"explicit orders"

The NKJV has "Did we not strictly command you not to teach in this name," which is a
Greek manuscript variant found in the Greek texts
אi2, D, and E,
but not in MSS P74, א*, A, or B. The
UBS4 puts the NKJV option in the text, but the negative "not" in brackets. This question expects
a "yes" answer. The Apostles were warned!

The construction is a Semitic idiom (cf. Luke 22:15) similar to the COGNATE ACCUSATIVE
in Koine Greek, where the VERB (parangellō) and the DIRECT OBJECT
(parangelia) are from the same root. This construction intensifies the basic meaning of the terms.
It is interesting that this term in the Koine papyri found in Egypt meant an official summons to court or
an order from a court (cf. Moulton and Milligan, Vocabulary of the Greek Testament, p. 481).

▣ "this man's" This expression shows the contempt of the Jewish leaders. They never
mention Jesus' name. The Talmud even calls Him "so and so" (cf. M. R. Vincent, Word Studies,
vol. 1, p. 234).

▣ "blood upon us" Peter and John were continuing to assert that these Jewish leaders
engineered Jesus' death (cf. Acts 5:30; 2:33; 3:14-15; 4:10). This was also Stephen's accusation
in Acts 7:52.

verses.zh: 彼得和众使徒回答说：「顺从　神，不顺从人，是应当的。
verses.en: But Peter and the apostles replied,[NOTE:1] “We must obey[NOTE:2] God rather than people.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “apostles answered and said.”
Obey. See 4:19. This response has Jewish roots (Dan 3:16-18; 2 Macc 7:2; Josephus, Ant. 17.6.3 [17.159]).
Here ἀνθρώποις (anthrōpois) has been translated as a generic noun (“people”).
verses.commentary:
5:29 "must" This word dei means moral necessity. This shows the Apostles' obligation to
preach the truth, regardless of the consequences (cf. Acts 4:19). See full note at Acts 1:16.

verses.zh: 你们挂在木头上杀害的耶稣，我们祖宗的　神已经叫他复活。
verses.en: The God of our forefathers[NOTE:1] raised up Jesus, whom you seized and killed by hanging him on a tree.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “ancestors”; Grk “fathers.”

Or “by crucifying him” (“hang on a tree” is by the time of the first century an idiom for crucifixion). The allusion is to the judgment against Jesus as a rebellious figure, appealing to the language of Deut 21:23. The Jewish leadership has badly “misjudged” Jesus.
verses.commentary:
5:30 "The God of our fathers" These early Christians believed they were the true spiritual
heirs and descendants of the OT people of God (cf. Acts 3:13; Rom. 2:28-29; Gal. 6:16; 1 Pet. 3:5,9;
Rev. 1:6). They were the new people of God, the new Israel!

▣ "raised up Jesus" The NT affirms that the Father raised Jesus (cf. Acts 2:24,32;
3:15,26; 4:10; 5:30; 10:40; 13:30,33,34,37; 17:31; Rom. 6:4,9) to confirm the truth of Jesus'
life and teachings. This is a major aspect of the Kerygma (cf. 1 Corinthians 15).

It should also be noted that the NT affirms that the Son and the Spirit were also involved
in this great affirmation event.

- the Son - John 2:19-22; 10:17-18

- the Spirit - Rom. 8:11

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

▣ "whom you had put to death by hanging Him on a cross" This relates back to the curse of
Deut. 21:23. These religious leaders wanted Jesus, a Messianic pretender, to bear the curse of YHWH. Jesus
bore the curse of the OT law (i.e., the soul that sins will surely die [cf. Ezek. 18:4,20] and all humans
have sinned, cf. Rom. 3:9-18, 23) for us (cf. Gal. 3:13; Col. 1:14). Jesus was the innocent lamb of God
who gave Himself for the estranged world (cf. Mark 10:45; John 1:29; 2 Cor. 5:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CRUCIFIXION

verses.zh: 神且用右手将他高举（或译：他就是　神高举在自己的右边），叫他作君王，作救主，将悔改的心和赦罪的恩赐给以色列人。
verses.en: God exalted him[NOTE:1] to his right hand as Leader[NOTE:2] and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “This one God exalted” (emphatic).
Or “Founder” (of a movement).
Or “to give repentance and forgiveness of sins to Israel.”
verses.commentary:
5:31 "God exalted to His right hand" This is a recurrent theme in Acts (cf. Acts 2:33; 3:21; 5:31; 7:55-56).

The term "exalted" is translated

- in John 3:14 as "lifted up"

- in Phil. 2:9 as "highly exalted"

The cross was Christ's means of exaltation and triumph (cf. Col. 1:15; 2 Cor. 2:14).

The anthropomorphic phrase "right hand" was imagery for the place of power and
authority (cf. Matt. 26:64; Acts 2:33-36; Rev. 22:1). God is an eternal Spirit. He does not have a physical body.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

▣ "Prince" This verse clearly and specifically asserts the Messiahship of Jesus. This same
term was used of Jesus in Acts 3:15, where it could be translated "Author" (NRSV). It can mean "chief,"
"pioneer," or "prince." It was also used in Koine Greek of the founder of a school or family (cf. Heb. 2:10; 12:2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: AUTHOR/LEADER

▣ "Savior" This title was used in the first century Greco-Roman world of Caesar. He claimed
to be the savior of culture and peace. Another term which the Caesars claimed for themselves, but Christians
used uniquely for Jesus, was Lord (kurios).

This term "Savior" was used in the OT as a title for YHWH (cf. 2 Sam. 22:3; Ps. 106:21;
Isa. 43:4,11; 45:15,21; 49:26; 60:16; 63:8). NT writers often assert the Deity of Jesus by attributing
to Him OT titles of YHWH. Notice how Paul in his letter to Titus does this (notice the Semitic parallelism).

- Titus 1:3, "God our Savior"

- Titus 1:4, "Christ Jesus our Savior"

- Titus 2:10, "God our Savior"

- Titus 2:13, "our great God and Savior, Christ Jesus"

- Titus 3:4, "God our Savior"

- Titus 3:6, "Jesus Christ our Savior"

SPECIAL TOPIC: OUR SAVIOR

▣ "to grant repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins" This shows the purpose of Jesus'
death (cf. Luke 24:47 and Acts 2:38). It is unusual for NT authors to refer to repentance as a gift
from God (cf. Acts 11:18 [to Gentiles]; 2 Tim. 2:25; and possibly also Rom. 2:4). Usually it is one
of the requirements of the New Covenant for the human recipient of the gospel (cf. Mark 1:15 and
Acts 3:16,19; 20:21). I think it is a literary way to show that God wants all humans made in His image
to be saved. It is not an issue related to God's sovereignty.

Often those who focus solely on God's part in the New Covenant use this verse to prove
that salvation is all of God and does not involve any participation on the part of mankind. However,
this is a good example of proof-texting a passage to fit one's preconceived system of theology (i.e., Calvinsim). The
Bible clearly asserts the priority and necessity of God's initiation, but also reveals that the concept
of "covenant" best describes His chosen model of how to relate to needy humanity. Freedom is a gift
which God gave in creation. God does not violate this gift/responsibility (cf. Rom. 2:4; 2 Cor. 7:10).
He does draw us, woo us, work with us, and provide a way of redemption (cf. John 6:44,65). But fallen
humans must respond and continue to respond in repentance, faith, obedience, and perseverance.

Here is an interesting quote from Frank Stagg, New Testament Theology, p. 119:

"Men cannot achieve but only receive repentance, yet they must
receive it. By faith a man receives Christ into his innermost person; and Christ,
as a transforming presence reverses the course of that life from self-trust to
trust in God, from self-assertion to self-denial. This conversion is the reversal
of the Fall, in which man sought to find the whole meaning of his existence
within himself."

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (NT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

verses.zh: 我们为这事作见证；　神赐给顺从之人的圣灵也为这事作见证。」
verses.en: And we are witnesses of these events,[NOTE:1] and so is the Holy Spirit whom God has given to those who obey[NOTE:2] him.”
notes: Or “things.” They are preaching these things even to the hostile leadership.
Those who obey. The implication, of course, is that the leadership is disobeying God.
verses.commentary:
5:32 Several times in Acts Peter referred to the fact that the Apostles and disciples are
witnesses of Jesus' life, death, and resurrection. In this context he adds, "the Holy Spirit"
as witness. This may be a way of affirming the two necessary OT witnesses to confirm a matter
(cf. Num. 35:30; Deut. 17:6; 19:15).

Luke/Acts speak of the gift of the Spirit

- at baptism - Acts 2:38

- at obedience to the gospel - Acts 5:32

- cannot be bought - Acts 8:19-20

- to the Gentiles - Acts 10:45; 11:17

- from the Father - Luke 11:13 (cf. James 1:17)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT (gift of. . .)

▣ "those who obey Him" The Apostles were obeying God but the Sanhedrin were not! What a
shocking statement.

Obedience is a lifestyle choice!

- We must obey by believing the gospel.

- We must continue in obedience to enjoy its fruits (cf. Matt. 7:24-27; Luke 6:46-48).

The rare term "obey" (peithomai plus archē, cf. Acts 27:21; Titus 3:1), used in Acts 5:29
and 32, was a combination of the terms "ruler" (archē) and obey.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

verses.zh: 公会的人听见就极其恼怒，想要杀他们。
verses.en: Now when they heard this, they became furious[NOTE:1] and wanted to execute them.[NOTE:2]
notes: The only other use of this verb for anger (furious) is Acts 7:54 after Stephen’s speech.
Wanted to execute them. The charge would surely be capital insubordination (Exod 22:28).
verses.commentary:
5:33

NASB
"they were cut to the quick"

NKJV
"they were furious"

NRSV, Peshitta
"they were enraged"

TEV
"they were so furious"

NJB
"this so infuriated them"

REB
"touched them on the raw"

This term literally means "cut with a saw" or "gnash with the teeth." This very
same term in the same form is also used in Stephen's sermon in Acts 7:54, where the added phrase, "cut to the
heart," shows the full emotional imagery (see also Luke 2:35). This strong term (i.e., diaprō) is
similar in meaning in Acts 2:37a.

▣ "intended to kill them" This is an IMPERFECT MIDDLE
(deponent) INDICATIVE, implying that

- they began at this point to try to kill them

- this was a recurrent plan and desire

From our knowledge of the early church's growth from Acts, #1 fits best. Notice it is the
Sadducees who expressed this anger and murderous intent. It is just possible that the Pharisees
(i.e., Gamaliel) saw the early church as a useful thorn to poke at the Sadducean rejection of
resurrection in general. Pharisees would not want to affirm the resurrection of Jesus, but would
affirm the concept of a resurrection followed by a future life with God.

It is surprising to modern Bible readers that religious leaders could plan murder.
Remember these were Sadducees committed to the writings of Moses, which commanded that a blasphemer
must be stoned to death. These leaders thought they were acting on God's behalf and in conformity
to His word (cf. Lev. 24:10-16).

verses.zh: 但有一个法利赛人，名叫迦玛列，是众百姓所敬重的教法师，在公会中站起来，吩咐人把使徒暂且带到外面去，
verses.en: But a Pharisee[NOTE:1] whose name was Gamaliel,[NOTE:2] a teacher of the law who was respected by all the people, stood up[NOTE:3] in the council[NOTE:4] and ordered the men to be put outside for a short time.
notes: A Pharisee was a member of one of the most important and influential religious and political parties of Judaism in the time of Jesus. There were more Pharisees than Sadducees (according to Josephus, Ant. 17.2.4 [17.42] there were more than 6,000 Pharisees at about this time). Pharisees differed with Sadducees on certain doctrines and patterns of behavior. The Pharisees were strict and zealous adherents to the laws of the OT and to numerous additional traditions such as angels and bodily resurrection.

Gamaliel was a famous Jewish scholar and teacher mentioned here in v. 34 and in Acts 22:3. He had a grandson of the same name and is referred to as “Gamaliel the Elder” to avoid confusion. He is quoted a number of times in the Mishnah, was given the highest possible title for Jewish teachers, Rabba (cf. John 20:16), and was highly regarded in later rabbinic tradition.
Grk “standing up in the council, ordered.” The participle ἀναστάς (anastas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.
Or “the Sanhedrin” (the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews).

verses.zh: 就对众人说：「以色列人哪，论到这些人，你们应当小心怎样办理。
verses.en: Then he said to the council,[NOTE:1] “Men of Israel,[NOTE:2] pay close attention to[NOTE:3] what you are about to do to these men.
notes: Grk “said to them”; the referent (the council) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Or “Israelite men,” although this is less natural English. The Greek term here is ἀνήρ (anēr), which only exceptionally is used in a generic sense of both males and females. In this context, it is highly unlikely that this is a generic usage, since Gamaliel was addressing the Sanhedrin, the Jewish high council, which would have been exclusively male.
Or “men, be careful.”

verses.zh: 从前杜达起来，自夸为大；附从他的人约有四百，他被杀后，附从他的全都散了，归于无有。
verses.en: For sometime ago[NOTE:1] Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody, and about 400 men joined him. He[NOTE:2] was killed, and all who followed him were dispersed and nothing came of it.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “For before these days.”
Grk “who.” The relative pronoun was replaced by the pronoun “he,” and a new sentence was begun in the translation at this point.
Grk “and they came to nothing.” Gamaliel’s argument is that these two insurrectionists were taken care of by natural events.
verses.commentary:
5:36-37 "Theudas. . .Judas of Galilee" Josephus mentions these same two names (cf. Antiq. 20.5.1).
However, he listed them in the reverse order. Further historical information shows that there were two
persons by this name who were Jewish zealots against Rome. Therefore, both the NT and Josephus could
be accurate. The one mentioned by Gamaliel rebelled in A.D. 6, whereas the one mentioned
by Josephus rebelled in A.D. 44.

verses.zh: 此后，报名上册的时候，又有加利利的犹大起来，引诱些百姓跟从他；他也灭亡，附从他的人也都四散了。
verses.en: After him Judas the Galilean arose in the days of the census[NOTE:1] and incited people to follow him in revolt.[NOTE:2] He too was killed, and all who followed him were scattered.
notes: Or “registration.”
The verb ἀφίστημι (aphistēmi) as a transitive means “cause to revolt” as used in Josephus, Ant. 8.7.5 (8.198), 20.5.2 (20.102); see BDAG 157 s.v. 1.
verses.commentary:
5:37 "in the days of the census" Josephus (cf. Antiq.18.1.1; Wars 2.8.1) tells us
that Augustus ordered a tax to be levied on the Jews, soon after Archelaus was dethroned and Quirinius
was made legate of Syria (i.e., about A.D. 6-7). These census for taxation purposes
occurred every fourteen years, but took years to complete.

▣ "Judas of Galilee" He is mentioned several times by Josephus (cf. Antiq. 18.1.1-6;
20.5.2 and also in Wars 2.8.1; 2.17.8-9). His revolt occurred in about A.D. 6 or 7. He
was the founder of the zealot movement. The zealots (Josephus calls them "the fourth philosophy" and
"the Sicarii" (i.e., assassins) are possibly the same political movement.

verses.zh: 现在，我劝你们不要管这些人，任凭他们吧！他们所谋的、所行的，若是出于人，必要败坏；
verses.en: So in this case I say to you, stay away from these men and leave them alone because if this plan or this undertaking originates with people,[NOTE:1] it will come to nothing,[NOTE:2]
notes: Here ἀνθρώπων (anthrōpōn) has been translated as a generic noun (“people”).
Or “it will be put to an end.”
verses.commentary:
5:38 "stay away from these men and let them alone" What surprising advice! This phrase has two
AORIST ACTIVE IMPERATIVES.

- aphistēmi, separate, put away

- aphiēmi, send away, dismiss

▣ "if" This is a THIRD CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which means potential
action or even probable action.

verses.zh: 若是出于　神，你们就不能败坏他们，恐怕你们倒是攻击　神了。」
verses.en: but if[NOTE:1] it is from God, you will not be able to stop them, or you may even be found[NOTE:2] fighting against God.” He convinced them,[NOTE:3]
notes: This is expressed in a first class condition, in contrast to the condition in v. 38b, which is third class. As such, v. 39 is rhetorically presented as the more likely option.

According to L&N 39.32, the verb εὑρεθῆτε (heurethēte, an aorist passive subjunctive) may also be translated “find yourselves”—“lest you find yourselves fighting against God.” The Jewish leader Gamaliel is shown contemplating the other possible alternative about what is occurring.

Grk “They were convinced by him.” This passive construction was converted to an active one (“He convinced them”) in keeping with contemporary English style. The phrase “He convinced them” is traditionally placed in Acts 5:40 by most English translations; the standard Greek critical text (represented by NA28 and UBS5) places it at the end of v. 39.
verses.commentary:
5:39 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE, which usually denotes an
affirmation of truth, but here it is used in a literary sense (i.e., not true to reality but to make a point).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII

▣ "or else you may even be found fighting against God" It must be remembered that these
religious leaders think they are acting on God's behalf. The very fact that Gamaliel speaks the possibility
of the Jewish leadership being sincerely wrong is a shocking statement (cf. Acts 11:17).

verses.zh: 公会的人听从了他，便叫使徒来，把他们打了，又吩咐他们不可奉耶稣的名讲道，就把他们释放了。
verses.en: and they summoned the apostles and had them beaten.[NOTE:1] Then[NOTE:2] they ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus and released them.
notes: Had them beaten. The punishment was the “forty lashes minus one,” see also Acts 22:19; 2 Cor 11:24; Mark 13:9. The apostles had disobeyed the religious authorities and took their punishment for their “disobedience” (Deut 25:2-3; m. Makkot 3:10-14). In Acts 4:18 they were warned. Now they are beaten. The hostility is rising as the narrative unfolds.

The word “Then” is supplied as the beginning of a new sentence in the translation. The construction in Greek has so many clauses (most of them made up of participles) that a continuous English sentence would be very awkward.
verses.commentary:
5:40 "They took his advice" This phrase is included in Acts 5:39 in some translations (cf. NRSV)
and in Acts 5:40 in others (cf. NASB, NKJV). The TEV and NJB keep it in Acts 5:39, but start a new paragraph.

▣ "flogged" This was not the same as the Roman flogging (mastix, cf. Acts 22:24-25),
which Jesus endured. This referred to the Jewish beating with rods (cf. Deut. 25:3; i.e., derō,
Luke 12:47-48; 20:10-11; 22:63). It was very painful, but not life-threatening.

The interpretive problem is that these two Greek terms are often used interchangeably.
The Septuagint of Deut. 25:3 has mastix, but it refers to a Jewish punishment. Luke regularly
uses derō for this Jewish synagogue beating (literally "skinning an animal").

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCOURGED

▣ "and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus" This same Council had done this earlier
(cf. Acts 4:17,21). This time they beat them and repeated the warning.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE NAME OF THE LORD

verses.zh: 他们离开公会，心里欢喜，因被算是配为这名受辱。
verses.en: So they left the council rejoicing because they had been considered worthy[NOTE:1] to suffer dishonor for the sake of the name.[NOTE:2]
notes: That is, considered worthy by God. They “gloried in their shame” of honoring Jesus with their testimony (Luke 6:22-23; 2 Macc 6:30).
The name refers to the name of Jesus (cf. 3 John 7).

verses.zh: 他们就每日在殿里、在家里不住地教训人，传耶稣是基督。
verses.en: And every day both in the temple courts[NOTE:1] and from house to house, they did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news[NOTE:2] that Jesus was the Christ.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “temple.” This is actually a reference to the courts surrounding the temple proper and has been translated accordingly.
Grk “teaching and evangelizing.” They were still obeying God, not men (see 4:18-20; 5:29).
See the note on Christ in 2:31.tn Or “Messiah”; both “Christ” (Greek) and “Messiah” (Hebrew and Aramaic) mean “one who has been anointed.”
verses.commentary:
5:42 "every day, in the temple" These early witnesses of Jesus refused to be silenced, even
in the very heart of Judaism, the temple in Jerusalem.

▣ "from house to house" The early church had their meetings in private homes spread
throughout the city (cf. Acts 2:46). There were no church buildings until several hundred years later.

NASB, NKJV
"the Christ"

NKJV, TEV, REB
"the Messiah"

In this Jewish setting the title "Messiah" is more appropriate (cf. Acts 2:31; 3:18;
5:42; 8:5; 9:22), as Peter used in Matt. 16:16. When Paul preached to Jews he also used this as a
reference to the promised, anointed One (cf. Acts 17:3; 18:5,28).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own
interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation.
You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of
the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why did the Apostles stay within Judaism so long?

- List the titles of Jesus and their meanings which are used in Acts 3.

- What are the two minimal requirements in salvation?

- Why is Moses quoted so often in the New Testament?

- What is the significance of the Abrahamic covenant to the NT church?

- Why were Peter and John arrested?

- Outline Peter's third sermon.

- What is significant about the prayer of Acts 4:24-31?

- To be truly New Testament must one be communistic? (cf. Acts 4:32)

- List the reasons why Luke included the account of Ananias and Sapphira.

- Did Ananias realize that he was filled with Satan? Did he realize that he had lied to God?

- Why was God seemingly so harsh?

- What about miracles (especially healings) in our day?

- Why were the Sadducees so mad?

- Why did the angel release the Apostles from prison?

- Outline Peter's fourth sermon. List the common elements between his other recorded sermons in Acts.

- Who was Gamaliel?

- Why should Christians rejoice in suffering?
